newsitem.title: PERU: Japan's Ikeda arrives to thank Peru's Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Ikeda arrives to thank Peru's Fujimori.

text.p: Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda arrived in Lima early on Thursday to congratulate President Alberto Fujimori and hear firsthand how Peru's military ended the 18-week-long hostage crisis.

Ikeda, who travelled with family members of the two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen who were among 71 hostages rescued in Tuesday's daring assault, was met by Peruvian Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi at Lima's military airport on his arrival soon after midnight local time (0500 GMT).
"His visit is to express thanks for the results of this operation to free the hostages from the house of the Japanese ambassador," Pandolfi told reporters.
Ikeda was due to attend the funeral on Thursday morning of Peru's Supreme Court justice Carlos Giusti, the only one of 72 hostages to die during Tuesday's raid.
He would later meet Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, the ill-fated host of the Dec. 17 cocktail party, and then Fujimori, Japanese foreign mininistry officials said.

In brief comments to reporters, Ikeda said he would discuss with Peruvian authorities how to avoid a repeat of the hostage crisis which saw a group of Marxist rebels hold Peruvian, Bolivian and Japanese VIPs for 126 days for ransom in exchange for jailed comrades.
In Tokyo, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he planned to visit Peru shortly to add his personal thanks to Fujimori for ending the hostage drama.
"I would like to thank Peru from the bottom of my heart for thoroughly preparing for the raid and successfully freeing most of the hostages," Hashimoto told the Lower House of parliament.

Tokyo had consistently urged Fujimori to seek a peaceful end to the standoff and was not informed of plans to storm the residence in advance. But Hashimoto has said he understands Fujimori's decision not to brief him.

During a visit of three or four days, Ikeda also planned to visit some of the two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen among the hostages, and offer his condolences to the families of Giusti and two soldiers killed in the rescue operation.
He was also due to supervise the re-opening of the Japanese Embassy in Lima.
Ikeda's delegation included 27 police officers, six members of a medical team and 10 relatives of freed Japanese captives.
Ikeda had previously visited Peru in the days after the takeover of the residence as Tokyo tried to restrain Fujimori from an immediate violent course of action.
All 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were killed in Tuesday's assault which ended Latin America's longest hostage siege.
